title: Type Guards & Narrowing
summary: **Type guards** are runtime checks (`typeof`, `instanceof`, `in`, truthiness) that *narrow* a broad type to a more specific one inside a block — and with custom guards (`x is Foo`) and assertion functions you can teach the compiler your own narrowing rules.

subtopics.title: typeof guards
subtopics.explanation: typeof narrows primitive types. Inside if (typeof x === 'string'), TypeScript knows x is a string and lets you call string methods safely. It recognizes the JavaScript typeof results: 'string', 'number', 'boolean', 'symbol', 'bigint', 'undefined', 'object', and 'function'. It is the go-to guard for union types that mix primitives.

subtopics.title: instanceof guards
subtopics.explanation: instanceof narrows to a class type by checking the prototype chain. Inside if (err instanceof TypeError), TypeScript treats err as a TypeError and exposes its members. Use it when discriminating between class instances — Error subclasses, Date, custom classes — rather than primitives.

subtopics.title: The in operator guard
subtopics.explanation: in narrows by checking whether a property exists on an object. if ('swim' in animal) tells TypeScript animal is the member of the union that has a swim method. It is ideal for object unions that lack a shared discriminant but have distinguishing properties.

subtopics.title: Truthiness narrowing
subtopics.explanation: A plain truthiness check narrows away null, undefined, '', 0, and NaN. if (value) inside the block removes null | undefined from value's type, so you can safely access it. This is the idiomatic way to guard optional values before use, but beware that 0 and '' are also falsy.
subtopics.example: if (user) console.log(user.name); // user is non-null here

subtopics.title: Equality narrowing
subtopics.explanation: Comparing with ===, !==, ==, or != narrows both operands to their common type. if (x === y) tells TypeScript x and y share a type in that branch; if (value !== null) removes null from value. Equality against literal types is the heart of discriminated-union narrowing.

subtopics.title: User-defined type guards (x is Foo)
subtopics.explanation: A function whose return type is a type predicate (param is Type) teaches TypeScript a custom narrowing rule. function isString(x: unknown): x is string { return typeof x === 'string' }. When it returns true, the compiler narrows the argument to that type in the caller. Use it to encapsulate reusable or complex checks.
subtopics.example: function isCat(a: Animal): a is Cat { return 'meow' in a; }

subtopics.title: Assertion functions
subtopics.explanation: An assertion function has return type 'asserts x is Type' (or 'asserts condition'). It throws if the condition fails and otherwise narrows x for all code after the call — no if-block needed. assertIsDefined(x) makes x non-null below the call. This mirrors Node's assert and centralizes invariants.
subtopics.example: function assertDefined<T>(v: T): asserts v is NonNullable<T> { if (v == null) throw new Error(); }

subtopics.title: Discriminated-union guards
subtopics.explanation: When every member of a union shares a literal discriminant field (kind, type, tag), checking that field narrows to the exact member. switch (shape.kind) { case 'circle': ... } gives you shape.radius in that case. This is the most robust narrowing pattern and is covered in depth in the discriminated unions topic.
subtopics.example: switch (s.kind) { case 'circle': return s.radius; case 'square': return s.side; }

foundations.overview: Type narrowing is how TypeScript refines a broad type (like a union or unknown) into a more specific one within a code branch, based on runtime checks called type guards. typeof, instanceof, in, truthiness, and equality are built-in guards; user-defined guards and assertion functions let you define your own. Narrowing is what makes union types ergonomic — you check, and the compiler grants you the precise type.
foundations.formalDefinition: A type guard is an expression that the compiler recognizes as evidence about a value's type, causing it to narrow that value's static type within the controlled scope. A user-defined guard is a function returning a type predicate (param is Type); an assertion function returns asserts param is Type and narrows by throwing on failure.
foundations.whyItMatters: Without narrowing, union and unknown types would be nearly unusable — you could not safely call any member. Narrowing is everywhere in real code that handles optional values, parsed JSON, error objects, and discriminated state. Interviewers use it to test whether you write safe branch logic instead of casting with as.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture the value's type as a set of possibilities; each guard removes the possibilities that fail the check, leaving a smaller, safer set inside the branch. A custom guard is you handing the compiler a proof it can trust.
foundations.browserPerspective: The guards themselves (typeof, instanceof, in, comparisons) are real JavaScript that runs in the browser; the narrowing is the compile-time interpretation of those checks. The type predicates and asserts annotations are erased — only the runtime check remains.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Safely accessing optional props after a truthiness check, handling unknown from JSON.parse, branching on Error subclasses in catch blocks, distinguishing API response variants, and validating untrusted input with reusable isX guards.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct narrowing converts a class of runtime 'cannot read property of undefined' crashes into compile-time errors, improving reliability and reducing production incidents and support load.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Reusable guards and assertion functions centralize validation logic, so teams stop scattering ad-hoc checks and casts and instead share trusted, named predicates that the compiler honors everywhere.
foundations.performanceImpact: Negligible runtime cost — guards are ordinary cheap comparisons. The predicate/asserts annotations are erased, so the only runtime work is the check you would have written anyway.
commonUseCases: Guarding optional/nullable values before access (truthiness, != null)
Branching on Error subclasses in catch blocks (instanceof)
Validating unknown JSON with reusable user-defined guards
Asserting invariants once with assertion functions

commonMisconceptions.myth: Casting with 'as' is the same as a type guard.
commonMisconceptions.reality: 'as' silences the compiler without any runtime check, so a wrong cast crashes at runtime; a guard performs a real check and narrows safely.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A function returning boolean automatically narrows its argument.
commonMisconceptions.reality: You must declare a type predicate (param is Type) — a plain boolean return does not narrow at the call site.

steps.name: Start broad
steps.detail: value has type string | number | null — three possibilities, none safe to use directly.

steps.detail: Inside if (value), null (and 0/'') are removed, leaving string | number for this branch.

steps.name: Use safely
steps.detail: Now value.toUpperCase() is allowed — the compiler knows it is a string.

codeLab.title: Write a user-defined guard isNonNull
codeLab.instructions: Implement isNonNull so its return type is a type predicate that narrows away null and undefined. Using it in Array.filter should give a fully non-null array.
hints: Change the return type from boolean to a type predicate.
Use value is NonNullable<T> so filter refines the array element type.

debuggingLab.title: A guard that returns boolean instead of a predicate
debuggingLab.symptom: After calling a custom check, the value is still treated as the broad union type and member access errors out — narrowing did not happen.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Because isCat is annotated to return boolean, the compiler treats it as an opaque truth test and does not refine animal. Inside the if-block animal stays Cat | Dog, so animal.meow() is rejected since Dog has no meow.
commonMistakes: Returning boolean from a guard instead of a type predicate.
Assuming any function with a true/false result narrows its argument.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Give isCat a type predicate return type so the if-block narrows animal to Cat.

theory.question: What is type narrowing and what built-in type guards does TypeScript provide?
theory.directAnswer: Narrowing is the compiler refining a broad type (a union, unknown, or nullable) into a more specific one inside a code branch, based on runtime checks called type guards. The built-in guards are typeof (for primitives), instanceof (for class instances), the in operator (for property presence), truthiness checks (removing null/undefined/falsy), and equality comparisons (===, !==), including against literal discriminants.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Compile-time refinement of a value's type within a scope, driven by runtime checks the compiler understands.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: So union and unknown types are usable — you can safely access members only after proving which type you have.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler interprets each guard as evidence and removes the union members that fail it, leaving a narrowed type for the controlled block; the guards are ordinary JavaScript that still runs.

theory.whyImportant: Narrowing is foundational to safe TypeScript and a frequent interview topic that separates casting (as) from real, checked branch logic.
theory.realWorldExample: In a catch block, if (err instanceof TypeError) narrows err so you can read TypeError-specific properties without casting.

nestedTopics.title: typeof vs instanceof
nestedTopics.explanation: typeof narrows primitives; instanceof narrows class instances via the prototype chain.

nestedTopics.title: in operator
nestedTopics.explanation: Narrows object unions by checking for a distinguishing property.

nestedTopics.title: Truthiness
nestedTopics.explanation: if (value) removes null, undefined, and other falsy values inside the block.

followUps.question: How is narrowing different from casting with as?
followUps.answer: Narrowing performs a real runtime check and is safe; as just asserts a type with no check, so a wrong as crashes at runtime.

followUps.question: Why can typeof not narrow to a specific class?
followUps.answer: typeof on any object returns 'object', so it cannot distinguish classes; use instanceof for that.

theory.question: What is a user-defined type guard and how does it differ from an assertion function?
theory.directAnswer: A user-defined type guard is a function whose return type is a type predicate (param is Type); when it returns true, the compiler narrows the argument to that type at the call site, so you branch with an if. An assertion function instead returns asserts param is Type: it throws when the condition fails and narrows the argument for all code after the call, with no if-block. Guards are for conditional branching; assertions are for enforcing invariants.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two ways to teach the compiler custom narrowing: a predicate-returning guard and a throw-on-failure assertion.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To encapsulate reusable or complex checks the built-in guards cannot express, and to centralize invariants.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: x is Type narrows in the true branch of the call; asserts x is Type narrows from the call onward because failure throws and execution would not continue. Both annotations are erased at emit.

theory.whyImportant: Showing you can write both — and choose correctly between branching and asserting — signals strong practical TypeScript skill.
theory.realWorldExample: assertIsUser(data) after JSON.parse throws on a malformed payload and otherwise lets the rest of the function treat data as a User.

nestedTopics.title: Type predicate
nestedTopics.explanation: param is Type is the return type that triggers call-site narrowing.

nestedTopics.title: asserts narrowing
nestedTopics.explanation: asserts param is Type narrows for code after the call by throwing on failure.

followUps.question: When would you prefer an assertion function over a guard?
followUps.answer: When a value MUST satisfy the type for the code to proceed (an invariant) and you want to narrow without nesting everything in an if-block.

scenario.question: A teammate parses untrusted JSON with JSON.parse and then casts the result with 'as ApiResponse', causing runtime crashes when the payload is malformed. How do you make this safe?
scenario.directAnswer: Replace the cast with a real runtime check via a user-defined type guard or assertion function. Type the parse result as unknown, then write isApiResponse(x): x is ApiResponse (or assertIsApiResponse) that verifies the required fields and types. Only after the guard passes do you treat the data as ApiResponse, so malformed payloads are caught and handled instead of crashing deeper in the code.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Swapping an unchecked cast for a validated guard at the trust boundary.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: as bypasses all checking, so untrusted data that does not match the type fails unpredictably at runtime.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: JSON.parse returns unknown; the guard inspects the runtime shape and narrows to the expected type only when it actually matches, otherwise the branch handles the error.

scenario.whyImportant: Trust boundaries (network, storage, user input) are exactly where casting is dangerous and guards pay off; this is a very common real-world bug.

nestedTopics.title: unknown over any
nestedTopics.explanation: Typing the parse result unknown forces a check before use.

nestedTopics.title: Schema validators
nestedTopics.explanation: Libraries like Zod generate guards/asserts plus the type from one schema.

followUps.question: Why not just use 'as' if you are confident in the API?
followUps.answer: as has no runtime effect, so a single API change or bad payload crashes with no protection; a guard fails gracefully at the boundary.

coding.question: Given a union of shapes with a 'kind' discriminant, write an area function that narrows on kind, and add an exhaustiveness check so adding a new shape is a compile error.
coding.thoughtProcess: Each shape shares a literal 'kind' field, so a switch on shape.kind narrows to the exact member in each case, giving me the right properties. For exhaustiveness, the default branch assigns shape to a variable of type never; if a new kind is added and not handled, shape is no longer never there, producing a compile error that forces me to handle it.
coding.lineByLine: The union shares a literal 'kind' discriminant. switch (shape.kind) narrows shape to the matching member per case, so shape.radius and shape.side are valid only where they exist. The default assigns shape to a never variable: when every kind is handled, shape is narrowed to never and this compiles; adding an unhandled kind breaks it, enforcing exhaustiveness.

alternativeApproaches.title: in operator instead of a discriminant
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Without a kind field you can narrow by property presence, but it is less robust than a shared literal discriminant.
alternativeApproaches.code: if ('radius' in shape) return Math.PI * shape.radius ** 2;

followUps.question: How does the never assignment enforce exhaustiveness?
followUps.answer: If all cases are handled, shape is narrowed to never in default and assigns fine; an unhandled variant makes shape non-never, so the assignment fails to compile.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Type guards live at trust boundaries and in domain logic: validation modules expose reusable isX guards and assertIsX functions that the rest of the app relies on, replacing scattered ad-hoc checks and casts. Discriminated-union narrowing structures state and message handling cleanly.
productionDeepDive.performance: Guards are ordinary, cheap runtime comparisons; the predicate and asserts annotations are erased, so there is no overhead beyond the check itself. The win is avoiding defensive re-checks elsewhere because the type is already proven.
productionDeepDive.security: Guards are the primary defense for untrusted input. Parsing to unknown and validating with a guard (or a schema validator like Zod) before use prevents trusting malformed network/storage/user data — something casting with as never does.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Centralize guards and assertions as named, tested utilities and reuse them across the codebase; pair discriminated unions with never-based exhaustiveness checks so adding a variant surfaces every place that must handle it.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Prefer narrowing over as casts everywhere, name guards by intent (isUser, isNonNull), and keep their bodies aligned with the type they claim — a guard that lies is worse than a cast. Use assertion functions for invariants to avoid deep nesting.
productionDeepDive.observability: Type errors from missing narrowing surface in the editor and CI via tsc --noEmit. Exhaustiveness checks turn 'forgot to handle a case' into a build failure, and guards that throw produce clear runtime errors at the boundary.

caseStudies.problem: Apps cast untrusted JSON with as, causing runtime crashes on malformed data.
caseStudies.solution: Schemas generate runtime validators that act as type guards/assertions and infer the static type from one definition.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: A small runtime validation cost in exchange for safe, single-source-of-truth typing at boundaries.
caseStudies.lessons: Guards and assertions, not casts, are how you safely bridge untyped runtime data into typed code.

keyTakeaways: Narrowing refines a broad type within a branch using type guards; built-ins are typeof, instanceof, in, truthiness, and equality.
User-defined guards return a type predicate (x is Foo) to teach the compiler custom narrowing at the call site.
Assertion functions (asserts x is Foo) throw on failure and narrow for all code after the call — ideal for invariants.
Prefer guards over 'as' casts: a guard performs a real runtime check, while as silences the compiler and can crash at runtime.
Discriminated-union narrowing plus a never-based exhaustiveness check is the most robust pattern (see the discriminated unions topic).
